subject: Accounting
title: Subsidiary Ledgers
description: A short lesson to help you apply Subsidiary Ledgers.

hook.text: A company has 500 customers who owe money. The general ledger shows one total. Who owes what?

buildup.text: Subsidiary ledgers break down a general ledger account into individual detail records.

discovery.text: The accounts receivable subsidiary ledger has a separate page for each customer's balance.

twist.text: The general ledger total must always match the sum of all subsidiary records—a built-in control.

climax.text: Without subsidiary ledgers, tracking who owes what and who's been paid would be impossible.

punchline.text: The total hides the details. Subsidiary ledgers reveal them.

quiz.question: What does a subsidiary ledger do?
options: Breaks down a general ledger account into individual details

details.summary: Subsidiary ledgers provide detailed breakdowns of summary accounts in the general ledger—such as individual customer balances within accounts receivable. This topic explains how subsidiary ledgers keep the general ledger clean while preserving transaction-level detail.
details.whyItMatters: The general ledger shows you the total receivables balance, but if a customer calls about their account, you need the subsidiary ledger to see their specific transactions and balance.
takeaways: The accounts receivable subsidiary ledger has a separate account for each customer
The total of all subsidiary ledger accounts must equal the general ledger control account balance
Subsidiary ledgers exist for receivables, payables, inventory, and fixed assets

faq.question: What is a subsidiary ledger?
faq.answer: A subsidiary ledger is a detailed record that breaks down a general ledger control account into individual accounts. For example, the accounts receivable subsidiary ledger contains a separate account for each customer, showing their individual balance and transactions.

faq.question: Why must subsidiary ledger totals match the general ledger?
faq.answer: The general ledger control account is the summary; the subsidiary ledger holds the detail. If they don't match, it means a transaction was recorded in one but not the other—an error that must be found and corrected before financial statements can be trusted.
